nodes.title: Number Theory
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Arithmetic questions on integers date to antiquity (Euclid, Diophantus). Modern number theory emerged with Gauss's *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801), linking congruences, quadratic forms, and cyclotomy.

**Landmarks:** Riemann's memoir on $\zeta(s)$ (1859); Hilbert's problems; the Langlands program; Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem (1995).

**References:** Hardy & Wright, *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers*; Ireland & Rosen; Serre, *A Course in Arithmetic*.

nodes.title: Prime Numbers
nodes.definition: A **prime** is a natural number $p > 1$ whose only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$. Equivalently, $p$ cannot be written as $ab$ with $1 < a, b < p$. The primes are the multiplicative building blocks of $\mathbb{Z}$: every integer $n \ge 2$ factors uniquely into primes (fundamental theorem of arithmetic).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Euclid (~300 BCE)** proved infinitely many primes. **Euler (1737)** introduced $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$ and the Euler product $\prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. **Hadamard & de la Vallée Poussin (1896)** proved the Prime Number Theorem.

**References:** Hardy & Wright Ch. 1–3; Ribenboim, *The Book of Prime Number Records*.

content.markdown: Primality testing (Miller–Rabin, AKS) and prime distribution (Prime Number Theorem, Riemann Hypothesis) connect arithmetic to analysis and cryptography.

nodes.title: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.definition: Fix a modulus $n \ge 2$. **Modular arithmetic** identifies integers that differ by a multiple of $n$, forming residue classes $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Addition and multiplication descend to well-defined operations; one studies congruences $a \equiv b \pmod{n}$ and invertibility modulo $n$ (when $\gcd(a,n)=1$).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Gauss (1801)** systematized congruences in *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*. **Euler** stated Fermat's little theorem and Wilson's theorem. Modern **RSA (1977)** encrypts using exponentiation in $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$.

**References:** Gauss, *Disquisitiones*; Silverman, *A Friendly Introduction to Number Theory*.

content.markdown: Quadratic reciprocity, primitive roots, and the Chinese remainder theorem organize computations modulo composite moduli.

nodes.title: Diophantine Equations
nodes.definition: A **Diophantine equation** is a polynomial equation (often in several variables) for which only integer or rational solutions are sought—named after Diophantus of Alexandria. Examples range from linear systems and Pell's equation $x^2 - Dy^2 = 1$ to the general problem of deciding solvability (Hilbert's tenth problem, undecidable).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Diophantus (~250 CE)** wrote *Arithmetica*; **Fermat** left marginal notes on integer solutions. **Mordell (1922)** conjectured finitely many rational points on curves of genus $\ge 2$ (proved by Faltings, 1983). **Matiyasevich (1970)** showed Hilbert's tenth problem is undecidable.

**References:** Mordell, *Diophantine Equations*; Hindry & Silverman, *Diophantine Geometry*.

content.markdown: Geometry of curves and abelian varieties (Mordell, Faltings) gives finiteness and structure results beyond naive search.

nodes.title: Modular Forms
nodes.definition: A **modular form** of weight $k$ is a holomorphic function $f$ on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ satisfying $f(\gamma z) = (cz+d)^k f(z)$ for all $\gamma = \binom{a\ b}{c\ d} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ (and a growth condition at cusps). Cusp forms vanish at $\infty$; Eisenstein series provide canonical counterexamples.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Klein, Poincaré, Dedekind** developed automorphic functions in the 19th century. **Hecke (1930s)** introduced operators and L-functions. **Taniyama–Shimura–Weil** conjectured elliptic curves arise from modular forms—central to Wiles (1995).

**References:** Diamond & Shurman, *A First Course in Modular Forms*; Serre, *A Course in Arithmetic*.

content.markdown: Hecke operators act on spaces of modular forms; eigenforms encode arithmetic data (L-functions, Galois representations).

nodes.title: Algebraic Number Theory
nodes.definition: **Algebraic number theory** studies finite extensions $K/\mathbb{Q}$ (number fields), their rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, ideals, class groups, and unit groups. It generalizes unique factorization via ideal factorization and connects Galois theory to arithmetic invariants (discriminant, ramification, zeta/L-functions of $K$).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Dedekind (1870s)** introduced ideals and factorization in $\mathcal{O}_K$. **Hilbert**'s *Zahlbericht* (1897) synthesized class field theory. **Artin (1927)** proved the reciprocity law. **Chevalley, Tate** developed modern adelic language.

**References:** Marcus, *Number Fields*; Neukirch, *Algebraic Number Theory*.

content.markdown: Local fields, adeles, and class field theory unify abelian extensions; the Langlands program extends these ideas non-abelianly.

nodes.title: Riemann Zeta
nodes.definition: The **Riemann zeta function** is $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}$ for $\mathrm{Re}(s) > 1$, analytically continued to $s \ne 1$ with a simple pole at $s=1$. The **Euler product** $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ links it to primes; its zeros control error terms in the Prime Number Theorem.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Euler (1737)** introduced the series and product. **Riemann (1859)** wrote the memoir *Über die Anzahl der Primzahlen* with analytic continuation and the functional equation. **Riemann Hypothesis** stated there has been no proof since.

**References:** Edwards, *Riemann's Zeta Function*; Iwaniec & Kowalski, *Analytic Number Theory*.

content.markdown: Functional equation, critical strip, and the Riemann Hypothesis (all nontrivial zeros on $\mathrm{Re}(s)=\frac{1}{2}$) remain the central open problem in analytic number theory.

nodes.title: Fermat's Last Theorem
nodes.definition: **Fermat's Last Theorem** asserts that the equation $x^n + y^n = z^n$ has no positive integer solutions when $n > 2$. Fermat claimed a proof in a 1637 margin note; the statement resisted proof for over 350 years until a proof via elliptic curves and modular forms.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Fermat (~1637)** stated the result. **Kummer (1847)** used cyclotomic fields for many exponents. **Wiles (1995)**, with Taylor, proved modularity of semistable elliptic curves, implying FLT. **Ribet (1986)** had reduced FLT to modularity via Frey curves.

**References:** Singh, *Fermat's Enigma*; Cornell, Silverman, Stevens (eds.), *Modular Forms and Fermat's Last Theorem*.

content.markdown: The proof passes through the Taniyama–Shimura conjecture (modularity of semistable elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$), Galois representations, and level lowering.

nodes.title: Algebraic Geometry
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Algebraic geometry studies solutions of polynomial equations as geometric objects. Classical projective geometry (19th c.) met commutative algebra (Noether, Hilbert); **Grothendieck (1960s)** recast the subject via schemes and topoi.

**Landmarks:** Riemann–Roch; Weil conjectures (proved by Deligne); minimal model program; moduli of curves and vector bundles.

**References:** Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*; Vakil, *The Rising Sea*; Mumford, *The Red Book*.

nodes.title: Schemes
nodes.definition: An **affine scheme** is $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ for a commutative ring $R$—its points are prime ideals, structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{Spec}\,R}$ remembers $R$. A **scheme** is a locally ringed space locally isomorphic to affine schemes, glued along open subschemes. This framework carries nilpotents, arithmetic (schemes over $\mathbb{Z}$), and functor-of-points perspectives.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Grothendieck & Dieudonné (1960–67)** developed the theory in *Éléments de géométrie algébrique* (EGA). **Serre**'s *FAC* (1955) introduced sheaves on varieties. **Hartshorne (1977)** became the standard graduate text.

**References:** Hartshorne Ch. II–III; Eisenbud & Harris, *The Geometry of Schemes*.

content.markdown: Morphisms of schemes correspond to ring homomorphisms in the opposite direction; fiber products exist and replace intersection theory in many settings.

nodes.title: Varieties
nodes.definition: An **algebraic variety** over a field $k$ is (roughly) a zero locus of polynomials in affine space $\mathbb{A}^n_k$ or projective space $\mathbb{P}^n_k$, equipped with the Zariski topology and a structure sheaf of regular functions. Irreducible varieties correspond to prime ideals; dimension, singularities, and morphisms are studied classically before passing to schemes.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Hilbert's Nullstellensatz** (1890s) links radical ideals to affine varieties. **Noether** pioneered ideal theory. **Zariski** topologized varieties; **Weil** and **Serre** bridged to modern sheaf methods.

**References:** Shafarevich, *Basic Algebraic Geometry*; Cox, Little, O'Shea, *Ideals, Varieties, and Algorithms*.

content.markdown: Projective varieties are compact (proper) in the Zariski sense; birational maps replace coordinate changes and blow-ups.

nodes.title: Sheaf Cohomology
nodes.definition: For a scheme $X$ and sheaf of $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules $\mathcal{F}$, **sheaf cohomology** $H^i(X, \mathcal{F})$ are derived functors of the global sections functor $\Gamma(X,-)$. They measure failure of local sections to glue globally; $H^1$ classifies extensions, higher $H^i$ enter Riemann–Roch and classification.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Leray** introduced sheaves; **Cartan** developed sheaf cohomology on manifolds. **Grothendieck (1957)** defined cohomology of abelian sheaves in Tôhoku; **Serre** used it for algebraic varieties. **Deligne** proved Weil conjectures using $\ell$-adic cohomology.

**References:** Hartshorne Ch. III; Grothendieck, *Tôhoku*; Milne, *Lectures on Étale Cohomology*.

content.markdown: Čech cohomology computes on open covers; for quasi-coherent sheaves on Noetherian schemes, cohomology agrees with derived functors.

nodes.title: Algebraic Curves
nodes.definition: An **algebraic curve** is a one-dimensional variety (or scheme of dimension 1). Smooth projective curves over $k$ are classified by genus $g$; divisors, line bundles, and the **Riemann–Roch theorem** relate functions to geometry. Over $\mathbb{C}$, compact Riemann surfaces are curves of genus $g$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Riemann (1857)** introduced genus and differentials. **Weil, Hasse** developed point-counting over finite fields. **Deligne–Mumford (1969)** compactified $\mathcal{M}_g$ via stable curves.

**References:** Fulton, *Algebraic Curves*; Arbarello, Cornalba, Griffiths, Harris, *Geometry of Algebraic Curves*.

content.markdown: Moduli spaces $\mathcal{M}_g$ parametrize curves of genus $g$; low-genus cases (0, 1, 2) have explicit models.

nodes.title: Birational Geometry
nodes.definition: **Birational geometry** studies varieties up to **birational equivalence**—isomorphism in codimension 1 after blowing up/cutting lower-dimensional subsets. The **minimal model program** seeks canonical representatives; **Mori theory** uses the cone of curves and contractions to classify higher-dimensional varieties.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Italian school** (Castelnuovo, Enriques, Severi) classified surfaces. **Mori (1980s)** introduced extremal ray theory. **Birkar, Cascini, Hacon, McKernan (2010)** proved finite generation of canonical rings in characteristic 0.

**References:** Kollár & Mori, *Birational Geometry of Algebraic Varieties*; Debarre, *Higher-Dimensional Algebraic Geometry*.

content.markdown: The flip theorem and abundance conjecture remain active frontiers; threefolds are largely settled, higher dimensions ongoing.

nodes.title: Elliptic Curves
nodes.definition: An **elliptic curve** over a field $k$ is a smooth projective curve of genus 1 with a chosen basepoint $O$, giving a group law via chord-and-tangent on points. Over $\mathbb{C}$, $E \cong \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$; over $\mathbb{Q}$, Mordell–Weil gives a finitely generated abelian group of rational points.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Weierstrass** parametrized elliptic functions. **Mordell (1922)** and **Weil (1928)** proved finite generation of rational points. **Tate** and **Silverman** systematized heights and BSD conjecture. **Wiles** used modularity of elliptic curves.

**References:** Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*; Husemöller, *Elliptic Curves*.

content.markdown: The $j$-invariant classifies curves over algebraically closed fields; isogenies and Tate modules link to modular forms and cryptography.

nodes.title: Algebraic Stacks
nodes.definition: An **algebraic stack** generalizes schemes to parametrize objects with automorphisms—quotients $[X/G]$ need not be schemes when stabilizers are nontrivial. Deligne–Mumford stacks are étale-locally quotients by finite group actions; Artin stacks allow more general quotients. They host moduli problems (curves, vector bundles, stable maps).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Deligne & Mumford (1969)** introduced DM stacks for $\mathcal{M}_g$. **Artin (1974)** defined Artin stacks via representability of diagonal. **Laumon & Moret-Bailly (2000)** wrote the standard reference.

**References:** Laumon & Moret-Bailly, *Champs algébriques*; Olsson, *Algebraic Spaces and Stacks*.

content.markdown: The inertia stack records automorphism groups; stacky curves and orbifolds appear in enumerative geometry and physics.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Probability arose from games of chance (Pascal, Fermat, 1654) and was axiomatized by **Kolmogorov (1933)** via measure theory. Stochastic processes model random evolution in time.

**Landmarks:** Law of large numbers; martingales (Doob); Brownian motion (Wiener, Lévy); Itô calculus; ergodic theory (Birkhoff).

**References:** Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*; Billingsley, *Probability and Measure*; Karatzas & Shreve, *Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus*.

nodes.title: Markov Chains
nodes.definition: A **Markov chain** $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ on a state space $S$ satisfies the **Markov property**: $\mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} \mid X_n, X_{n-1}, \ldots) = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1} \mid X_n)$. Transition probabilities $P_{ij} = \mathbb{P}(X_{n+1}=j \mid X_n=i)$ form a stochastic matrix (discrete) or kernel (continuous).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Markov (1906)** studied chains arising in Russian literature analysis. **Kolmogorov** gave rigorous foundations. **Doob** and **Chung** developed potential theory and limit theorems for chains.

**References:** Norris, *Markov Chains*; Levin, Peres, Wilmer, *Markov Chains and Mixing Times*.

content.markdown: Stationary distributions, recurrence/transience, and mixing rates connect to linear algebra and spectral gap questions.

nodes.title: Random Walk
nodes.definition: A **random walk** is $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ with i.i.d. increments $X_i$ (often mean zero). On $\mathbb{Z}^d$, recurrence depends on dimension ($d=1,2$ recurrent, $d \ge 3$ transient). Scaling limits connect to Brownian motion via Donsker's invariance principle.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Pólya (1921)** proved recurrence in $d=2$. **Donsker (1951)** proved functional CLT to Brownian motion. **Spitzer**, *Principles of Random Walk*, is a classic.

**References:** Spitzer, *Principles of Random Walk*; Lawler, *Random Walk: A Modern Introduction*.

content.markdown: Reflection principle, ballot problems, and gambler's ruin are classical tools; on graphs, random walks interact with spectral geometry of the Laplacian.

nodes.title: Martingales
nodes.definition: A **martingale** $(M_n, \mathcal{F}_n)$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = M_n$ (fair game). **Submartingales** grow on average; **supermartingales** shrink. Optional stopping, Doob decomposition, and martingale convergence theorems underpin stochastic analysis and financial mathematics.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Lévy** introduced martingales implicitly. **Doob (1953)** systematized the theory in *Stochastic Processes*. **Meyer** developed continuous-time theory and quadratic variation.

**References:** Williams, *Probability with Martingales*; Doob, *Stochastic Processes*.

content.markdown: Uniform integrability and $L^p$ bounds control convergence; martingale CLT generalizes sums of dependent variables.

nodes.title: Brownian Motion
nodes.definition: **Brownian motion** $(B_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a continuous stochastic process with $B_0=0$, independent Gaussian increments $B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, t-s)$, and continuous paths a.s. It is a Markov process, a martingale, and has quadratic variation $[B]_t = t$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Brown (1827)** observed pollen motion. **Einstein (1905)** and **Smoluchowski** explained it statistically. **Wiener (1923)** constructed continuous paths rigorously. **Lévy** studied fine properties of paths.

**References:** Karatzas & Shreve; Revuz & Yor, *Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion*.

content.markdown: Paul Lévy's characterization: continuous martingale with $B_0=0$ and $[B]_t = t$. Reflection principle solves hitting-time problems.

nodes.title: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.definition: The **Central Limit Theorem** states: if $X_i$ are i.i.d. with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2 < \infty$, then $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. Normalized sums become Gaussian regardless of the underlying distribution (under mild conditions).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**de Moivre (1733)** for binomial counts. **Laplace** and **Gauss** developed error theory. **Lindeberg (1922)** and **Feller** gave modern formulations. **Donsker** proved invariance principle.

**References:** Feller, *An Introduction to Probability Theory* Vol. II; Durrett, *Probability: Theory and Examples*.

content.markdown: Lindeberg and Lyapunov conditions weaken independence; functional CLT (Donsker) upgrades to path-space convergence.

nodes.title: Stochastic Calculus
nodes.definition: **Stochastic calculus** integrates with respect to Brownian motion via the **Itô integral** $\int H_s \, dB_s$, defined as an $L^2$ limit of simple processes. **Itô's lemma** is the chain rule for $f(B_t)$: $df = f'\,dB + \frac{1}{2}f''\,dt$. **SDEs** $dX_t = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dB_t$ model dynamics in finance and physics.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Itô (1944)** built stochastic integration. **Kunita & Watanabe (1967)** extended theory. **Black–Scholes (1973)** applied SDEs to option pricing. **Karatzas & Shreve** is the standard reference.

**References:** Karatzas & Shreve; Øksendal, *Stochastic Differential Equations*.

content.markdown: Stratonovich integral differs by a correction term; semimartingales generalize integrators beyond Brownian motion.

nodes.title: Ergodic Theory
nodes.definition: **Ergodic theory** studies measure-preserving transformations $T: X \to X$ on probability spaces. A system is **ergodic** if every invariant set has measure 0 or 1; then time averages along orbits equal space averages: $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(T^k x) \to \int f \, d\mu$ a.e.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Boltzmann** coined ergodic hypothesis. **Birkhoff (1931)** proved pointwise ergodic theorem. **von Neumann** proved mean ergodic theorem. **Kolmogorov** introduced entropy; **Ornstein** classified Bernoulli shifts.

**References:** Walters, *An Introduction to Ergodic Theory*; Einsiedler & Ward, *Ergodic Theory*.

content.markdown: Mixing, entropy (Kolmogorov–Sinai), and Oseledets multiplicative ergodic theorem link to chaotic dynamics and random matrix products.

nodes.title: Analysis & PDEs
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Calculus (Newton, Leibniz) matured into rigorous analysis (Cauchy, Weierstrass, Riemann). **Lebesgue (1902)** revolutionized integration; **Hilbert, Banach, von Neumann** founded functional analysis. PDEs unify physics and geometry (Laplace, Fourier, Maxwell, Einstein).

**Landmarks:** Spectral theorem; Sobolev spaces (1930s); distributions (Schwartz); elliptic regularity; Nash–Moser techniques.

**References:** Rudin, *Real and Complex Analysis*; Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*; Brezis, *Functional Analysis*.

nodes.title: Banach Spaces
nodes.definition: A **Banach space** is a complete normed vector space $(X, \|\cdot\|)$—every Cauchy sequence converges. Bounded linear operators $T: X \to Y$ form $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$; the Hahn–Banach theorem extends functionals; uniform boundedness and open mapping theorems are pillars of functional analysis.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Banach (1922)** wrote *Théorie des opérations linéaires*. **Hilbert** preceded with sequence spaces. **Riesz** and **Hausdorff** developed normed and metric ideas. **Banach–Steinhaus** and **Banach–Alaoglu** are foundational.

**References:** Brezis, *Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and PDEs*; Conway, *A Course in Functional Analysis*.

content.markdown: Examples: $L^p$, $C(K)$, sequence spaces $\ell^p$; dual spaces and weak topologies encode convergence modes.

nodes.title: Sobolev Spaces
nodes.definition: **Sobolev spaces** $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ consist of functions (or distributions) on a domain $\Omega$ whose weak derivatives up to order $k$ lie in $L^p$. Embeddings $W^{k,p} \hookrightarrow L^q$ or $C^{m,\alpha}$ control regularity; trace theorems restrict functions to boundaries.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Sobolev (1935)** introduced the spaces in the USSR. **Gagliardo–Nirenberg** proved interpolation inequalities. **Morrey** and **Rellich–Kondrachov** proved compact embeddings.

**References:** Adams & Fournier, *Sobolev Spaces*; Evans, *PDE* Ch. 5.

content.markdown: Weak formulations of PDEs seek solutions in $H^1$; Lax–Milgram gives existence for coercive bilinear forms.

nodes.title: Elliptic PDEs
nodes.definition: An **elliptic PDE** has no real characteristic directions—e.g. $-\Delta u = f$ or $Lu = f$ with $L$ uniformly elliptic. Solutions enjoy maximum principles, interior regularity (bootstrapping), and uniqueness under boundary conditions. The Laplace and Poisson equations are prototypical.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Laplace (1780s)** studied harmonic functions. **Schauder (1930s)** proved Hölder regularity. **Lax–Milgram (1954)** gave variational existence. **Gilbarg & Trudinger** is the standard reference.

**References:** Gilbarg & Trudinger, *Elliptic PDEs of Second Order*; Jost, *Partial Differential Equations*.

content.markdown: Fredholm alternative governs solvability on compact domains; spectral theory of the Laplacian links to geometry.

nodes.title: Heat Equation
nodes.definition: The **heat equation** $\partial_t u = \Delta u$ (or $u_t - \kappa \Delta u = 0$) is parabolic: information diffuses infinitely fast but smooths instantly. On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the fundamental solution is the Gaussian heat kernel; maximum principle gives uniqueness and comparison.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Fourier (1822)** solved heat flow via series. **E. E. Holmes** and **Duhamel** developed Green's functions. **John** and **Friedman** studied parabolic regularity and Harnack inequalities.

**References:** Evans, *PDE* Ch. 2; Friedman, *Partial Differential Equations of Parabolic Type*.

content.markdown: Feynman–Kac represents solutions as Brownian expectations; semigroup theory generates evolution $e^{t\Delta}$.

nodes.title: Wave Equation
nodes.definition: The **wave equation** $u_{tt} = c^2 \Delta u$ is hyperbolic: disturbances propagate at finite speed $c$ along characteristics. d'Alembert's formula solves 1D; energy $E(t) = \int (u_t^2 + c^2 |\nabla u|^2)$ is conserved for suitable boundary conditions.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**d'Alembert (1747)** solved vibrating strings. **Kirchhoff** gave explicit 3D solutions. **Hadamard** classified PDEs by characteristics. **Lax–Phillips** developed scattering theory.

**References:** Evans, *PDE* Ch. 2; Taylor, *Partial Differential Equations* Vol. I.

content.markdown: Finite propagation distinguishes hyperbolic from parabolic/elliptic; shock formation appears in nonlinear variants.

nodes.title: Fourier Analysis
nodes.definition: **Fourier analysis** decomposes functions into superpositions of $e^{2\pi i \xi x}$ (or $\sin, \cos$). The **Fourier transform** $\hat{f}(\xi) = \int f(x) e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$ diagonalizes convolution; **Plancherel** gives $\|f\|_2 = \|\hat{f}\|_2$ on $L^2$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Fourier (1807)** introduced series for heat. **Plancherel (1910)** proved $L^2$ isometry. **Carleson (1966)** proved pointwise convergence of Fourier series for $L^2$. **Stein** unified harmonic analysis.

**References:** Stein & Shakarchi, *Fourier Analysis*; Katznelson, *An Introduction to Harmonic Analysis*.

content.markdown: Poisson summation, uncertainty principle, and Tauberian theorems connect to number theory and probability.

nodes.title: Spectral Theory
nodes.definition: **Spectral theory** studies operators via their **spectrum** $\sigma(T)$—eigenvalues and generalized spectrum. Self-adjoint operators on Hilbert space admit spectral theorem (projection-valued measures); compact operators have discrete spectrum accumulating at 0.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Hilbert** coined "spectrum" for integral equations. **von Neumann** developed spectral theorem (1929–32). **Dunford** introduced functional calculus. **Reed & Simon** *Methods of Mathematical Physics* is canonical.

**References:** Reed & Simon, Vol. I; Conway, *A Course in Operator Theory*.

content.markdown: Resolvent $(T-\lambda)^{-1}$, spectral radius, and functional calculus $f(T)$ extend matrix diagonalization to infinite dimensions.

nodes.title: Hilbert Spaces
nodes.definition: A **Hilbert space** is a complete inner-product space $(H, \langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$. Orthogonality, Riesz representation ($\phi \mapsto \langle \cdot, v\rangle$), and orthonormal bases characterize $H$. $L^2$ is the prime example; quantum states are unit vectors in Hilbert space.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Hilbert (1912)** formalized integral equations with quadratic forms. **Riesz–Fischer (1907)** proved $L^2$ completeness. **von Neumann** placed QM on Hilbert space foundations.

**References:** Rudin, *Real and Complex Analysis* Ch. 4; Halmos, *Introduction to Hilbert Space*.

content.markdown: Projection onto closed convex sets minimizes distance; spectral theorem applies to normal operators.

nodes.title: Measure Theory
nodes.definition: A **measure space** $(X, \mathcal{M}, \mu)$ has a $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{M}$ of measurable sets and a countably additive measure $\mu$. Carathéodory extension builds measures from outer measures; Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ extends length; integration is defined via simple functions and limits.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Lebesgue (1902)** defined measure and integral. **Carathéodory (1914)** gave axiomatic extension. **Kolmogorov (1933)** axiomatized probability as measure. **Halmos** and **Rudin** are standard expositions.

**References:** Rudin, *Real and Complex Analysis*; Folland, *Real Analysis*.

content.markdown: Fubini–Tonelli interchange integrals; Radon–Nikodym derivatives relate absolutely continuous measures.

nodes.title: Lebesgue Integration
nodes.definition: **Lebesgue integration** integrates measurable $f$ via $\int f\,d\mu = \sup \int \varphi\,d\mu$ over simple $\varphi \le f$. **Dominated convergence** passes limits through integrals; **monotone convergence** handles increasing sequences. More functions are integrable than in Riemann theory.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Lebesgue (1902)** in his thesis. **Fatou** and **Lebesgue** proved convergence theorems. **Riesz–Fischer** linked $L^2$ to Fourier series. **Bartle** gives an accessible treatment.

**References:** Bartle, *The Elements of Integration and Lebesgue Measure*; Folland, *Real Analysis*.

content.markdown: Almost everywhere (a.e.) statements replace pointwise exceptions; $L^1$ completeness enables functional analysis.

nodes.title: $L^p$ Spaces
nodes.definition: For a measure space $(X,\mu)$, **$L^p(X,\mu)$** ($1 \le p < \infty$) consists of measurable $f$ with $\|f\|_p = (\int |f|^p)^{1/p} < \infty$, modulo a.e. zero. **Hölder** and **Minkowski** inequalities control products and sums; $L^2$ is Hilbert; $L^\infty$ is the essential supremum norm.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Riesz (1910)** introduced $L^p$ in his work on integral equations. **Hausdorff** and **Young** developed inequalities. **Stein** treats $L^p$ in harmonic analysis.

**References:** Folland, *Real Analysis* Ch. 6; Brezis, *Functional Analysis*.

content.markdown: Dual $(L^p)^* \cong L^q$ for $1 < p < \infty$ (Riesz representation); interpolation (Riesz–Thorin) connects exponents.

nodes.title: Distributions
nodes.definition: A **distribution** (generalized function) is a continuous linear functional on $\mathcal{D}$ (smooth compactly supported test functions). Derivatives $\langle T', \varphi\rangle = -\langle T, \varphi'\rangle$ extend classical differentiation; the Dirac delta $\delta$ picks out $\varphi(0)$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Dirac (1920s)** used delta functions in QM. **Schwartz (1945–50)** created distribution theory and won the Fields Medal (1950). **Friedlander** and **Hörmander** applied to PDEs.

**References:** Friedlander & Joshi, *Introduction to the Theory of Distributions*; Hörmander, *The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators* Vol. I.

content.markdown: Fourier transform extends to tempered distributions $\mathcal{S}'$; fundamental solutions of PDEs are often distributions.

nodes.title: Complex Analysis
nodes.definition: A function $f: U \subset \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ is **holomorphic** if it is complex-differentiable (equivalently analytic, satisfying Cauchy–Riemann equations). **Cauchy integral formula** $f(z_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint \frac{f(z)}{z-z_0}dz$ forces infinite differentiability; **residue theorem** evaluates contour integrals.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Cauchy (1825)** developed complex integration. **Riemann (1851)** founded geometric function theory. **Weierstrass** emphasized power series. **Ahlfors (1979)** *Complex Analysis* is a classic.

**References:** Ahlfors, *Complex Analysis*; Conway, *Functions of One Complex Variable*.

content.markdown: Liouville, maximum modulus, and Schwarz lemma constrain global behavior; Riemann mapping theorem classifies simply connected domains.

nodes.title: Topology & Geometry
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Topology emerged from Euler (polyhedra, Königsberg bridges) and **Poincaré's Analysis Situs (1895)**. Algebraic topology (homotopy, homology) and differential geometry (Riemann, 1854) unified geometry with algebra and analysis.

**Landmarks:** Fundamental group; singular homology (Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms); de Rham theorem; Milnor's exotic spheres; Perelman's Poincaré proof.

**References:** Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*; Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*; do Carmo, *Riemannian Geometry*.

nodes.title: Fundamental Group
nodes.definition: The **fundamental group** $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ is homotopy classes of loops $\gamma: [0,1] \to X$ based at $x_0$, with concatenation. It is a functor from pointed spaces to groups; van Kampen's theorem computes $\pi_1$ of glued spaces.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Poincaré (1895)** introduced the fundamental group in *Analysis Situs*. **van Kampen (1933)** gave the gluing formula. **Seifert–van Kampen** is standard in textbooks.

**References:** Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology* Ch. 1; Massey, *A Basic Course in Algebraic Topology*.

content.markdown: Simply connected means $\pi_1 = 0$; covering spaces correspond to subgroups of $\pi_1$.

nodes.title: Homology
nodes.definition: **Singular homology** $H_n(X)$ measures $n$-dimensional holes: $H_0$ counts path components, $H_1$ abelianizes $\pi_1$, $H_n$ for $n \ge 2$ records higher cycles. It is homotopy invariant, functorial, and satisfies the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms (including exactness and excision).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Poincaré** defined Betti numbers. **Noether** promoted homology as groups. **Eilenberg & Steenrod (1945)** axiomatized homology theories. **Singular homology** (Eilenberg) is the standard construction.

**References:** Hatcher Ch. 2; Spanier, *Algebraic Topology*.

content.markdown: Betti numbers $\beta_n = \mathrm{rank}\, H_n$ summarize complexity; universal coefficient theorem relates coefficients.

nodes.title: Smooth Manifolds
nodes.definition: An $n$-dimensional **smooth manifold** $M$ is a Hausdorff paracompact space locally homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$, with a **smooth atlas**—compatible charts $\phi: U \to \mathbb{R}^n$. Tangent bundles $TM$, vector fields, and differential forms live intrinsically on $M$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Riemann (1854)** introduced abstract manifolds. **Whitney (1936)** proved embedding theorems. **Milnor (1956)** discovered exotic 7-spheres. **Lee** and **Spivak** are modern references.

**References:** Lee, *Introduction to Smooth Manifolds*; Spivak, *A Comprehensive Introduction to Differential Geometry*.

content.markdown: Whitney embedding theorem places smooth $n$-manifolds in $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$; partitions of unity glue local data globally.

nodes.title: Differential Topology
nodes.definition: **Differential topology** studies smooth manifolds up to diffeomorphism—transversality makes intersections clean; **degree theory** counts preimage points; **cobordism** relates manifolds as boundaries. Sard's theorem and Whitney tricks are basic tools.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Whitney** developed transversality and embeddings. **Milnor** wrote *Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint* (1965). **Thom** founded cobordism theory (Fields Medal 1958). **Kervaire–Milnor** classified exotic spheres.

**References:** Milnor, *Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint*; Guillemin & Pollack, *Differential Topology*.

content.markdown: Surgery theory classifies manifolds in high dimensions; handle decompositions build manifolds inductively.

nodes.title: Riemannian Geometry
nodes.definition: A **Riemannian manifold** $(M,g)$ has a smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space. The **Levi-Civita connection** is torsion-free and metric-compatible; **curvature** (Riemann, Ricci, scalar) measures deviation from flatness; **geodesics** locally minimize length.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Riemann (1854)** introduced metric geometry. **Levi-Civita (1917)** and **Cartan** developed connections. **Einstein (1915)** used Ricci curvature in GR. **do Carmo** and **Petersen** are standard texts.

**References:** do Carmo, *Riemannian Geometry*; Petersen, *Riemannian Geometry*.

content.markdown: Gauss–Bonnet links curvature to topology; comparison theorems (Bonnet–Myers, Cartan–Hadamard) constrain global shape.

nodes.title: Knot Theory
nodes.definition: A **knot** is a smooth embedding $K: S^1 \hookrightarrow S^3$ up to ambient isotopy. **Invariants** (Jones, Alexander, HOMFLY polynomials; knot group; signature) distinguish knots. **Concordance** and **cable operations** organize the knot concordance group.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Tait (1870s)** tabulated knots. **Alexander (1920s)** introduced the polynomial. **Jones (1984)** discovered his polynomial via von Neumann algebras. **Witten (1989)** linked Jones to Chern–Simons theory.

**References:** Lickorish, *An Introduction to Knot Theory*; Rolfsen, *Knots and Links*.

content.markdown: Three-manifold invariants (Heegaard Floer, Khovanov homology) modernized classical knot polynomials.

nodes.title: Covering Spaces
nodes.definition: A **covering map** $p: \tilde{X} \to X$ is a local homeomorphism evenly covering neighborhoods. Deck transformations $\mathrm{Aut}(p)$ act on fibers; for connected $X$, coverings correspond to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $\pi_1(X, x_0)$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Poincaré** and **Riemann** used covering ideas implicitly. **Seifert** classified coverings via $\pi_1$. **Hatcher** Ch. 1 gives the modern treatment.

**References:** Hatcher Ch. 1; Massey, *Algebraic Topology* Ch. 5.

content.markdown: Universal cover $\tilde{X}$ corresponds to the trivial subgroup; Galois coverings match normal subgroups.

nodes.title: CW Complexes
nodes.definition: A **CW complex** is built inductively: start with 0-cells (points), attach $n$-cells via attaching maps $S^{n-1} \to X^{(n-1)}$. Cellular homology computes homology from the combinatorics of cells; CW structures exist on most spaces of interest.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Whitehead (1949)** introduced CW complexes. **Milnor** used them in homotopy theory. **Hatcher** develops cellular homology in Ch. 2.

**References:** Hatcher Ch. 2; Spanier, *Algebraic Topology*.

content.markdown: Homotopy extension and cellular approximation simplify maps between CW complexes.

nodes.title: Singular Cohomology
nodes.definition: **Singular cohomology** $H^n(X; R)$ is cohomology of the dual cochain complex $\mathrm{Hom}(C_\bullet(X), R)$. The **cup product** $\smile$ gives a graded ring structure; **universal coefficient** relates $H^n(X; R)$ to $H_n(X)$ and $\mathrm{Ext}$ terms.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Alexander & Whitney (1935)** introduced cup product. **Eilenberg & Steenrod** axiomatized cohomology. **Mac Lane** developed cup product algebraically.

**References:** Hatcher Ch. 3; Spanier, *Algebraic Topology*.

content.markdown: Cohomology is representable by Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces; characteristic classes live in $H^*(X; \mathbb{Z})$.

nodes.title: de Rham Cohomology
nodes.definition: **de Rham cohomology** $H^k_{dR}(M) = \ker d / \mathrm{im}\, d$ on the complex of differential forms on a smooth manifold $M$. Closed forms modulo exact forms; Poincaré lemma shows locally exact = exact on contractible sets.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**de Rham (1931)** introduced the cohomology. **de Rham theorem (1950s):** $H^k_{dR}(M) \cong H^k_{sing}(M; \mathbb{R})$. **Hodge (1940s)** developed harmonic forms. **Bott & Tu** is a classic exposition.

**References:** Bott & Tu, *Differential Forms in Algebraic Topology*; Warner, *Foundations of Differentiable Manifolds*.

content.markdown: Hodge theory on compact Riemannian manifolds picks canonical representatives—harmonic forms.

nodes.title: Vector Bundles
nodes.definition: A **vector bundle** $E \to B$ locally looks like $U \times \mathbb{R}^k$: fibers $E_b$ vary continuously (smoothly) over base $B$. Sections, connections, and curvature generalize calculus on manifolds; **characteristic classes** (Chern, Pontryagin, Stiefel–Whitney) are cohomological obstructions.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Whitney (1930s)** founded bundle theory. **Chern (1946)** introduced Chern classes. **Atiyah–Singer index theorem (1963)** linked analysis to topology via bundles.

**References:** Hatcher, *Vector Bundles and K-Theory*; Steenrod, *The Topology of Fibre Bundles*.

content.markdown: Associated bundles build from group representations; tangent and cotangent bundles are canonical examples.

nodes.title: Algebra
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Modern algebra crystallized from Galois's work on equations (1832), **Noether's** ideal theory, and **van der Waerden's** *Moderne Algebra* (1930). Groups encode symmetry; rings and modules unify number theory and geometry.

**Landmarks:** Sylow theorems; structure of finite groups; Galois correspondence; homological algebra; representation theory of Lie groups.

**References:** Dummit & Foote, *Abstract Algebra*; Lang, *Algebra*; Atiyah & Macdonald, *Introduction to Commutative Algebra*.

nodes.title: Groups
nodes.definition: A **group** $(G, \cdot)$ is a set with an associative binary operation, identity $e$, and inverses $g^{-1}$ for each $g \in G$. Groups model symmetry: permutations, rotations, Galois groups, and Lie groups. Subgroups, cosets, and quotient groups $G/N$ organize structure; Lagrange's theorem relates orders.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Galois (1832)** linked groups to solvability of equations. **Cayley (1854)** gave abstract definition. **Jordan** and **Sylow** developed finite group theory. **Gorenstein** led the classification program.

**References:** Dummit & Foote Ch. 1–6; Rotman, *An Introduction to the Theory of Groups*.

content.markdown: Simple groups are building blocks; classification of finite simple groups (1980s) is a monumental theorem.

nodes.title: Representation Theory
nodes.definition: **Representation theory** studies homomorphisms $\rho: G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$ (or algebra representations), linearizing symmetry. Irreducible representations are atoms; character theory $\chi(g) = \mathrm{tr}\,\rho(g)$ detects decomposition on finite groups over $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Frobenius & Burnside (1890s–1900s)** developed character theory. **Weyl (1920s)** treated compact Lie groups. **Serre**'s *Linear Representations of Finite Groups* is concise and deep.

**References:** Serre, *Linear Representations of Finite Groups*; Fulton & Harris, *Representation Theory*.

content.markdown: Peter–Weyl theorem decomposes $L^2$ on compact Lie groups; highest weight theory classifies representations of semisimple Lie algebras.

nodes.title: Galois Theory
nodes.definition: **Galois theory** links field extensions $L/K$ to groups $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ of $K$-automorphisms of $L$. The **fundamental theorem** is a lattice anti-isomorphism between intermediate fields and subgroups. Solvability by radicals corresponds to solvable Galois groups (Abel, Galois).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Galois (1832)** died at 20, leaving manuscripts on solvability. **Abel (1824)** proved quintic unsolvability. **Artin** reframed Galois theory abstractly. **Emil Artin's** *Galois Theory* lectures remain classic.

**References:** Artin, *Galois Theory*; Cox, *Galois Theory*.

content.markdown: Over $\mathbb{Q}$, splitting fields of polynomials encode root symmetries; inverse Galois problem asks which groups arise.

nodes.title: Commutative Algebra
nodes.definition: **Commutative algebra** studies commutative rings $R$ and $R$-modules: ideals, localization $S^{-1}R$, Noetherian rings (ascending chain condition), primary decomposition, and dimension theory (Krull dimension). It is the local language of algebraic geometry via $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Noether (1921)** proved primary decomposition in Noetherian rings. **Krull** developed dimension and localization. **Zariski** connected algebra to geometry. **Atiyah & Macdonald (1969)** is the concise bible.

**References:** Atiyah & Macdonald; Eisenbud, *Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry*.

content.markdown: Regular sequences, depth, and Cohen–Macaulay rings measure singularities; flatness governs base change.

nodes.title: Rings & Modules
nodes.definition: A **ring** has addition (abelian group), multiplication (associative, distributive), often with unit. **Modules** are abelian groups with scalar action $r \cdot m$; kernels and quotients behave like vector spaces without basis. **Exact sequences** track how maps fit; **Artin–Wedderburn** classifies semisimple rings.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Dedekind** introduced ideals in number rings. **Noether** pioneered module theory. **Wedderburn (1907)** classified semisimple algebras. **Jacobson** developed radical theory.

**References:** Dummit & Foote Ch. 10–12; Lam, *Lectures on Modules and Rings*.

content.markdown: Noncommutative algebra studies quivers, group algebras, and operator algebras; modules unify linear algebra over rings.

nodes.title: Homological Algebra
nodes.definition: **Homological algebra** studies chain complexes and derived functors in abelian categories. **Ext**$^n_R(M,N)$ measures extension obstructions; **Tor**$_n^R(M,N)$ measures failure of flatness. Projective/injective resolutions compute them; **snake lemma** and **five lemma** propagate exactness.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Cartan & Eilenberg (1956)** wrote the founding text. **Grothendieck** developed abelian categories in Tôhoku. **Mac Lane** and **Rotman** give accessible introductions.

**References:** Weibel, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*; Rotman, *An Introduction to Homological Algebra*.

content.markdown: Derived categories (Verdier) abstract resolutions; spectral sequences (Leray–Serre) compute composed functors.

nodes.title: Tensor Products
nodes.definition: The **tensor product** $M \otimes_R N$ is the universal bilinear $R$-module: maps $M \times N \to P$ bilinear factor through $M \otimes_R N$. Base change $M \otimes_R S$ extends scalars; **flat** modules preserve exact sequences under $-\otimes_R M$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Whitney** used tensors in differential geometry. **Bourbaki** systematized universal constructions. **Atiyah–Macdonald** treats tensor products for commutative algebra.

**References:** Atiyah & Macdonald Ch. 2; Dummit & Foote Ch. 10.

content.markdown: In geometry, tensors on manifolds are sections of tensor products of bundles; universal property replaces coordinates.

nodes.title: Lie Algebras
nodes.definition: A **Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{g}$ is a vector space with bilinear bracket $[\cdot,\cdot]$ that is antisymmetric and satisfies the **Jacobi identity** $[x,[y,z]] + [y,[z,x]] + [z,[x,y]] = 0$. Lie algebras are infinitesimal symmetries of Lie groups; semisimple classification via root systems (Dynkin diagrams).
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Lie, Killing, Cartan (1880s–1900s)** classified semisimple Lie algebras. **Weyl, Harish-Chandra** developed representation theory. **Humphreys** and **Hall** are standard texts.

**References:** Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*; Hall, *Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations*.

content.markdown: Universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ connects to representation theory; Killing form detects semisimplicity.

nodes.title: Category Theory
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** **Eilenberg & Mac Lane (1942–45)** invented categories, functors, and natural transformations to formalize "natural" constructions in algebraic topology—especially in the comparison of singular and simplicial homology.

**Landmarks:** Yoneda lemma; adjoint functors; Grothendieck topoi (1960s); categorical logic; higher categories (quasi-categories, $\infty$-categories).

**References:** Mac Lane, *Categories for the Working Mathematician*; Awodey, *Category Theory*; Riehl, *Category Theory in Context*; Leinster, *Basic Category Theory*.

nodes.title: Categories
nodes.definition: A **category** $\mathcal{C}$ has objects $\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})$, morphisms $\mathrm{Hom}(A,B)$ with **composition** (associative) and **identities** $\mathrm{id}_A$. Every mathematical structure with structure-preserving maps forms a category (groups, rings, topological spaces, schemes). Commutative diagrams express coherence of multiple morphisms.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Eilenberg & Mac Lane (1945)** — *General theory of natural equivalences* introduced categories, functors, and natural transformations.

**See also:** Mac Lane (1998); Leinster, *Basic Category Theory*; Awodey, *Category Theory*.

content.markdown: Small vs. large categories: set-theoretic issues are managed via universes or careful foundations.

nodes.title: Functors
nodes.definition: A **functor** $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ assigns objects $F(A)$ and morphisms $F(f): F(A) \to F(B)$, preserving composition and identities. **Covariant** functors preserve direction; **contravariant** reverse it ($F: \mathcal{C}^{op} \to \mathcal{D}$). Faithful, full, and essentially surjective functors measure how faithfully $\mathcal{C}$ embeds in $\mathcal{D}$.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Eilenberg & Mac Lane** defined functors in 1945. **Kan (1958)** developed left/right Kan extensions. **Mac Lane**'s *CTM* is the standard reference.

**References:** Mac Lane, *CTM* Ch. II; Riehl, *CT in Context* Ch. 1.

content.markdown: Forgetful functors drop structure; free functors adjoin it—often forming adjoint pairs.

nodes.title: Natural Transformations
nodes.definition: A **natural transformation** $\eta: F \Rightarrow G$ between functors assigns morphisms $\eta_A: F(A) \to G(A)$ such that for every $f: A \to B$, the **naturality square** commutes: $G(f) \circ \eta_A = \eta_B \circ F(f)$. Natural isomorphisms identify functorially equivalent constructions.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Eilenberg & Mac Lane (1945)** introduced naturality to make precise when a construction is "canonical." **Mac Lane** developed 2-categorical ideas. **Riehl** emphasizes naturality in proofs.

**References:** Mac Lane, *CTM* Ch. I; Riehl, *CT in Context* Ch. 1.

content.markdown: Natural transformations are the 2-morphisms of the 2-category **Cat**; representability uses natural bijections.

nodes.title: Limits & Colimits
nodes.definition: A **limit** of a diagram $D: \mathcal{J} \to \mathcal{C}$ is a universal cone—products, equalizers, pullbacks are examples. **Colimits** are universal cocones: coproducts, coequalizers, pushouts. Existence of all (co)limits of a given shape makes $\mathcal{C}$ complete/cocomplete.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Kan (1958)** developed limits in general. **Grothendieck** used fiber products and limits heavily in EGA. **Mac Lane** Ch. III; **Riehl** Ch. 3 give modern treatments.

**References:** Mac Lane, *CTM* Ch. III; Riehl, *CT in Context* Ch. 3.

content.markdown: Preservation of limits characterizes adjoints: right adjoints preserve limits; left adjoints preserve colimits.

nodes.title: Adjoint Functors
nodes.definition: An **adjunction** $F \dashv G$ means natural isomorphism $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(F(X), Y) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, G(Y))$. Unit $\eta: \mathrm{id} \Rightarrow GF$ and counit $\varepsilon: FG \Rightarrow \mathrm{id}$ satisfy triangle identities. Free–forgetful pairs and currying are archetypes.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Kan (1958)** formalized adjoints. **Lawvere** emphasized adjunctions in categorical logic. **Mac Lane** Ch. IV; **Awodey** gives an accessible account.

**References:** Mac Lane, *CTM* Ch. IV; Awodey, *Category Theory* Ch. 9.

content.markdown: Adjoints determine each other up to unique natural isomorphism; they preserve (co)limits in the correct direction.

nodes.title: Yoneda Lemma
nodes.definition: The **Yoneda embedding** $Y: \mathcal{C} \to [\mathcal{C}^{op}, \mathbf{Set}]$, $A \mapsto h_A = \mathrm{Hom}(-, A)$, is fully faithful. The **Yoneda lemma**: natural transformations $\mathrm{Nat}(h_A, F) \cong F(A)$—an object is determined by how other objects map into it.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Yoneda (1954)** introduced the embedding. **Grothendieck** and **Kan** developed functor categories in the 1950s–60s. The lemma is central to modern algebraic geometry (functor of points).

**References:** Mac Lane, *CTM* Ch. III; Riehl, *CT in Context* Ch. 2.

content.markdown: Representable functors are building blocks; presheaf categories are universal colimits completions.

nodes.title: Topos Theory
nodes.definition: An **elementary topos** is a category with finite limits, exponentials $B^A$, and a **subobject classifier** $\Omega$ (internal truth object). Topoi model **higher-order intuitionistic logic**; sheaves on a site form a Grothendieck topos, unifying geometry and logic.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Grothendieck (1960s)** introduced Grothendieck topoi for étale cohomology. **Lawvere & Tierney (1970)** axiomatized elementary topoi. **Johnstone**'s *Sketches of an Elephant* is the comprehensive treatise.

**References:** Johnstone, *Sketches of an Elephant*; Mac Lane & Moerdijk, *Sheaves in Geometry and Logic*.

content.markdown: Classifying topoi encode theories; forcing in set theory can be viewed topologically via topoi.

nodes.title: Logic
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Origins:** Logic formalizes valid reasoning. **Frege (1879)** and **Peano** gave predicate calculus; **Hilbert**'s program sought consistency proofs. **Gödel (1930–31)** proved completeness and incompleteness, reshaping foundations.

**Landmarks:** Model theory (Tarski, Robinson); forcing (Cohen); computability (Turing); type theory (Martin-Löf) and proof assistants.

**References:** Enderton, *A Mathematical Introduction to Logic*; Marker, *Model Theory*; Troelstra & van Dalen, *Constructivism in Mathematics*.

nodes.title: First-Order Logic
nodes.definition: **First-order logic** has formulas built from atomic predicates $P(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$, connectives $\land,\lor,\neg,\to$, and quantifiers $\forall x$, $\exists x$ over individual variables. Structures $\mathcal{M}$ interpret symbols; $\mathcal{M} \models \varphi$ means $\varphi$ is true in $\mathcal{M}$; proofs are syntactic derivations in a Hilbert or natural deduction system.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Frege (1879)** *Begriffsschrift* invented predicate logic. **Hilbert & Ackermann (1928)** systematized first-order systems. **Tarski** defined truth in models (1930s).

**References:** Enderton, *A Mathematical Introduction to Logic*; Mendelson, *Introduction to Mathematical Logic*.

content.markdown: First-order logic is expressive enough for most mathematics yet enjoys compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem phenomena.

nodes.title: Completeness Theorem
nodes.definition: **Gödel's completeness theorem (1929):** every first-order sentence $\varphi$ that is **valid** (true in all models, $\models \varphi$) is **provable** ($\vdash \varphi$) in a sound, complete proof system. Equivalently, consistent theories have models; satisfiability and consistency coincide for first-order logic.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Gödel (1929)** proved completeness in his dissertation. **Henkin (1949)** gave a model-existence proof via term models. **Completeness fails** for second-order logic.

**References:** Enderton Ch. 2; Marker, *Model Theory* Ch. 1.

content.markdown: Soundness ($\vdash \varphi \Rightarrow \models \varphi$) is easier; completeness is the deep direction via maximal consistent sets or Henkin constructions.

nodes.title: Compactness Theorem
nodes.definition: **Compactness:** if every finite subset of a first-order theory $T$ has a model, then $T$ has a model. Equivalently, if $T \models \varphi$, then some finite $T_0 \subset T$ already entails $\varphi$. Nonstandard models of arithmetic and ultraproducts rely on compactness.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Gödel** (via completeness) and **Malcev (1936)** applied compactness. **Tarski** popularized semantic methods. **Robinson** used it for nonstandard analysis.

**References:** Marker, *Model Theory* Ch. 2; Hodges, *A Shorter Model Theory*.

content.markdown: Proof routes: completeness + König's lemma, or ultraproducts via Łoś's theorem.

nodes.title: Model Theory
nodes.definition: **Model theory** studies classes of structures $\mathrm{Mod}(T)$ for first-order theories $T$: types, saturation, stability, quantifier elimination, and definability. **Morley's theorem** classifies uncountably categorical theories; o-minimality tame real geometry.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Tarski (1930s)** defined truth and decidability of real closed fields. **Morley (1965)** proved categoricity theorem. **Shelah** developed stability theory. **Marker** is a standard graduate text.

**References:** Marker, *Model Theory*; Hodges, *Model Theory*.

content.markdown: Connections to algebra: model-complete fields, differential fields, and Zilber's program for complex exponentiation.

nodes.title: Gödel Incompleteness
nodes.definition:
**Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931):** (1) Any consistent, effectively axiomatized theory $T$ extending Peano arithmetic (PA) is **incomplete**—there exists $\varphi$ with $T 
vdash \varphi$ and $T 
vdash 
eg\varphi$. (2) Such $T$ cannot prove its own consistency (if consistent). Self-reference via Gödel numbering is the mechanism.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Gödel (1931)** published *Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze*. **Rosser (1936)** strengthened to Rosser's sentence. **Turing** and **Church** linked undecidability to computability.

**References:** Enderton Ch. 3; Smith, *An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems*.

content.markdown: Incompleteness is not a flaw of mathematics but a fundamental limit of formal systems rich enough for arithmetic.

nodes.title: Type Theory
nodes.definition: **Type theory** classifies terms by types: $a : A$ means $a$ is a term of type $A$. **Dependent types** $\Pi_{x:A} B(x)$ internalize $\forall x:A, B(x)$; $\Sigma_{x:A} B(x)$ internalizes $\exists$. The **Curry–Howard correspondence** identifies proofs with programs and propositions with types.
nodes.historyAndReferences:
**Russell (1908)** types avoided paradoxes. **Church (1940)** typed $\lambda$-calculus. **Martin-Löf (1970s–80s)** developed constructive dependent type theory. **HoTT Book (2013)** linked types to homotopy theory.

**References:** Homotopy Type Theory collective, *The HoTT Book*; Nordström, Petersson, Smith, *Martin-Löf's Type Theory*.

content.markdown: Martin-Löf type theory (MLTT) underlies Agda, Coq, and Lean proof assistants; homotopy type theory adds identity types as paths.

edges.label: mod p
edges.theorem: Primes and primality testing are studied modulo n; Fermat's little theorem links primes to modular exponentiation.

edges.label: encodes
edges.theorem: The Euler product ζ(s) = ∏(1 − p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ directly encodes the distribution of prime numbers.

edges.label: via
edges.theorem: Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem by showing certain elliptic curves (Taniyama–Shimura) cannot have certain Galois representations.

edges.label: used in proof
edges.theorem: Modular forms and their Galois representations are central to Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

edges.label: generalizes
edges.theorem: Classical Galois theory over ℚ generalizes to Galois groups of number fields and their abelian extensions.

edges.label: generalizes
edges.theorem: An irreducible algebraic variety corresponds to a reduced, irreducible scheme of finite type over a field.

edges.label: built from
edges.theorem: Affine schemes are Spec(R) for commutative rings R; general schemes are glued from these.

edges.label: group law mod n
edges.theorem: The group law on elliptic curves reduces modulo n and underlies elliptic-curve cryptography.

edges.label: Wiles
edges.theorem: Wiles's modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves over ℚ implies Fermat's Last Theorem.

edges.label: on
edges.theorem: Sheaf cohomology (e.g. H^i(X, 𝒪_X)) is defined for schemes and measures global sections obstructions.

edges.label: discrete version
edges.theorem: A random walk on a graph with transition probabilities is a Markov chain on the vertex set.

edges.label: scaling limit
edges.theorem: Donsker's invariance principle: properly scaled random walks converge in distribution to Brownian motion.

edges.label: drives
edges.theorem: Stochastic calculus is built on Brownian motion as the fundamental continuous-time noise process.

edges.label: Itô
edges.theorem: Itô's integral is defined for martingale integrators; Brownian motion is a square-integrable martingale.

edges.label: related
edges.theorem: The CLT explains why Brownian motion arises as a limit of scaled random walks with finite-variance steps.

edges.label: Feynman-Kac
edges.theorem: The Feynman–Kac formula represents solutions of the heat equation as expectations of functionals of Brownian motion.

edges.label: weak solutions
edges.theorem: Weak solutions of elliptic PDEs live in Sobolev spaces W^{1,2}; Lax–Milgram gives existence in H¹₀.

edges.label: solve
edges.theorem: The heat equation on ℝⁿ is solved explicitly by convolving with the Gaussian heat kernel (Fourier method).

edges.label: operators on
edges.theorem: Spectral theory studies the spectrum σ(T) of bounded and unbounded operators on Banach and Hilbert spaces.

edges.label: Hurewicz
edges.theorem: **Hurewicz theorem:** For a path-connected space X, the first homology group satisfies H₁(X; ℤ) ≅ π₁(X)^ab (abelianization). More generally, if πᵢ(X) = 0 for i < n, then πₙ(X) ≅ Hₙ(X) for n ≥ 2.

edges.label: add metric
edges.theorem: A Riemannian manifold is a smooth manifold together with a smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space.

edges.label: dual viewpoints
edges.theorem: Homology Hₙ and cohomology Hⁿ are dual: for nice spaces, Hⁿ(X; R) ≅ Hom(Hₙ(X), R). Cup product in cohomology pairs with the Kronecker pairing with homology cycles.

edges.label: linearize
edges.theorem: Representation theory replaces abstract group elements with concrete matrices, preserving the group structure.

edges.label: Galois group
edges.theorem: The Galois group Gal(L/K) is a group of field automorphisms fixing K; it encodes the symmetry of roots.

edges.label: Spec
edges.theorem: The functor Spec assigns to a commutative ring R the affine scheme whose points are prime ideals of R.

edges.label: functors of points
edges.theorem: Schemes can be viewed as functors of points (functors from rings to sets), a categorical perspective on geometry.

edges.label: Lie groups
edges.theorem: Finite-dimensional representations of a Lie group are related to representations of its Lie algebra via differentiation.

edges.label: Mordell-Weil
edges.theorem: The Mordell–Weil theorem: the group of rational points on an elliptic curve over a number field is finitely generated.

edges.label: stationary
edges.theorem: A stationary distribution of a Markov chain is an invariant measure; ergodicity implies uniqueness and mixing.

edges.label: eigenvalues
edges.theorem: Eigenvalues of the Laplacian on a domain determine frequencies of vibration and appear in elliptic spectral theory.

edges.label: defines integral
edges.theorem: Lebesgue integration is defined with respect to a measure on a measurable space.

edges.label: builds
edges.theorem: $L^p$ spaces are spaces of equivalence classes of measurable functions integrable with respect to μ.

edges.label: $L^2$ case
edges.theorem: When $p=2$, $L^2$ is a Hilbert space with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle = \int f\bar{g}\,d\mu$.

edges.label: complete normed
edges.theorem: Every Hilbert space is a Banach space; functional analysis studies operators on such spaces.

edges.label: leads to
edges.theorem: Soundness and completeness connect syntactic provability with semantic validity in first-order logic.

edges.label: implies
edges.theorem: Completeness together with König's lemma yields the compactness theorem for first-order logic.

edges.label: tool
edges.theorem: Compactness is the engine behind nonstandard models, ultraproducts, and many model-theoretic constructions.

edges.label: maps between
edges.theorem: Functors are the structure-preserving maps between categories.

edges.label: 2-morphisms
edges.theorem: Natural transformations are morphisms in the functor category $[\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D}]$.

edges.label: preservation
edges.theorem: Right adjoints preserve limits; left adjoints preserve colimits.

edges.label: represented by
edges.theorem: The Yoneda embedding is fully faithful; representable functors are central to adjunctions.

edges.label: correspondence
edges.theorem: Connected covering spaces of $X$ correspond to subgroups of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$.

edges.label: computes
edges.theorem: Cellular homology of a CW complex computes singular homology and is efficient for computations.

edges.label: dual
edges.theorem: Singular cohomology is homotopy invariant and pairs with homology via the Kronecker product.

edges.label: de Rham theorem
edges.theorem: **de Rham:** $H^k_{dR}(M) \cong H^k_{sing}(M; \mathbb{R})$ for smooth manifolds $M$.

edges.label: forms on
edges.theorem: de Rham cohomology is defined using differential forms on smooth manifolds.

edges.label: specializes
edges.theorem: Commutative algebra studies commutative rings and their modules as in algebraic geometry.

edges.label: Ext & Tor
edges.theorem: Homological algebra measures failure of exactness via derived functors of Hom and tensor.

edges.label: unitary reps
edges.theorem: Peter–Weyl and representation theory of compact groups act on Hilbert spaces of $L^2$ functions.

edges.label: singular
edges.theorem: Singular homology is computed via chain complexes; homological algebra provides the algebraic language.

edges.label: sheaves
edges.theorem: Sheaf cohomology is a derived functor in the abelian category of sheaves of modules.

edges.label: abelian categories
edges.theorem: Homological algebra is developed in abelian categories; chain complexes form a functorial framework.

edges.label: functor of points
edges.theorem: The Yoneda philosophy: a scheme is determined by its functor of points on commutative rings.

edges.label: internal logic
edges.theorem: A topos has an internal higher-order logic; models of theories can be studied via classifying topoi.

edges.label: categorical semantics
edges.theorem: Cartesian closed categories and toposes provide semantics for typed λ-calculus and dependent type theory.

edges.label: Sobolev embeddings
edges.theorem: Sobolev spaces control regularity of functions whose derivatives appear in de Rham and PDE theory.

edges.label: associated
edges.theorem: Vector bundles associated to group representations; linkage between linear algebra and topology.

edges.label: local coefficients
edges.theorem: Tensor products assemble local data into global sections; vector bundles are families of vector spaces.

edges.label: fields
edges.theorem: Model theory of fields: quantifier elimination for algebraically closed fields, connections to Galois theory.

edges.label: transform on
edges.theorem: The Fourier transform is a unitary operator on $L^2$; holomorphic functions satisfy Cauchy–Riemann equations.

edges.label: weak derivatives
edges.theorem: Sobolev spaces and distributions unify weak formulations of PDEs.

edges.label: Laplace–Beltrami
edges.theorem: The Laplace–Beltrami operator on a Riemannian manifold generalizes the Laplacian in spectral geometry.

edges.label: Lie groups
edges.theorem: Lie algebras are the infinitesimal generators of Lie group actions on manifolds.

edges.label: one-object
edges.theorem: A group is the same data as a category with one object and invertible morphisms.

edges.label: undecidability
edges.theorem: Gödel's ideas on undecidability echo in algorithmic questions about Galois groups and diophantine problems.

edges.label: Wiener measure
edges.theorem: Brownian motion is built from a probability measure on path space; stochastic analysis uses measure theory.

edges.label: Galois connections
edges.theorem: Galois correspondences are adjunctions between posets of subgroups and subfields.

edges.label: fiber products
edges.theorem: Fiber products of schemes are pullbacks in the category of schemes; fundamental in intersection theory.
